name: Kahayan
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Perbedaan tekanan, nada, tempo, dan jeda sejauh data yang diperoleh tampaknya sama sekali tidak membedakan arti. Dengan demikian, fonem suprasegmental dalam BK tidak dikenal, paling tidak menjadi aspek yang perlu dibicarakan dalam bagian fonologi. Secara fonetis kata-kata dalam BK diucapkan dengan pola tekanan utama pada suku kedua dari depan. Pelanggaran terhadap pola itu akan menimbulkan semacam kejanggalan, seperti kebiasaan para pendeta gereja Kristen yang memberikan tekanan berpola pada suku kedua dari belakang. Contoh: /ha'i/ 'besar' /pa'hai/ 'besarkan' /ta'pahai/ ... /mam'pahai/ 'membesarkan' /ka'rambang/ 'pagar' /ta'karambang/ ... /ta'pakarambang/ 'terpagarkan' /ha'lamantek/ 'lintah' /ba'halamantek/ 'berlintah' *(') tanda tekanan
new_statements.translation: Differences of stress, pitch, tempo and pause, as far as the data obtained show, apparently do not distinguish meaning at all. Thus suprasegmental phonemes are unknown in BK [Bahasa Kahayan], or at least are not an aspect that needs discussion in the phonology section. Phonetically, words in BK are pronounced with a pattern of main stress on the second syllable from the beginning. Violating that pattern produces a kind of awkwardness, like the habit of the Christian church pastors who give patterned stress on the second syllable from the end. Examples: /ha'i/ 'big', /pa'hai/ 'enlarge!', /ta'pahai/ 'bigger than expected', /mam'pahai/ 'to enlarge', /ka'rambang/ 'fence', /ta'karambang/ 'unintentionally fenced', /ta'pakarambang/ 'fenced', /ha'lamantek/ 'leech', /ba'halamantek/ 'having leeches'. *(') = stress mark.
new_statements.citation: Durasid, Durdje; Djantera Kawi; Aries Djinal. 1990. Struktur Bahasa Kahayan. Jakarta: Pusat Pembinaan dan Pengembangan Bahasa, Departemen Pendidikan dan Kebudayaan.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive (no suprasegmental phonemes). Phonetically the main word stress falls on the second syllable counted from the beginning of the word (peninitial), regardless of word length or prefixation: the nine marked examples place the stress mark before syllable 2 in 2-, 3-, 4- and 5-syllable words (ha-ˈi, ka-ˈram-bang, ta-ˈka-ram-bang, ta-ˈpa-ka-ram-bang, ba-ˈha-la-man-tek), so in longer prefixed words stress lands on the antepenult or earlier, not the penult. The authors explicitly contrast this with penultimate stress, which they attribute to church pastors' (mission-Ngaju) pronunciation and call awkward-sounding.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (only 'tekanan utama' = main stress is described).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The only qualification is that penultimate stress occurs as a learned/church habit ('kebiasaan para pendeta gereja Kristen') and is judged deviant. P. 9 adds that suprasegmentals are omitted from the transcription because they are not phonemic.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms; examples include mono-morphemic roots and prefixed derivatives (ta-, mam-, ba-, tapa-), showing the count starts at the left edge of the prefixed word. Impressionistic (no instrumental data). NB: this conflicts with the penultimate-stress statements for Pulopetak Ngaju (Hardeland 1858; Mihing & Stokhof 1977) already in the catalog under ngaj1237, and with Kaufman & Himmelmann's impression of 'remarkably even prominence' in Ngaju; the Kahayan record should carry a caution flag rather than be merged silently with ngaj1237.
new_statements.identity_note: kaha1240 is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid for the retired ISO code [xah] Kahayan, merged into Ngaju [nij] (ngaj1237) by CR 2007-184 (2008). Durasid, Kawi & Djinal 1990 describe 'bahasa Kahayan (BK)', which they themselves equate with Dayak Ngaju / bahasa Kapuas ('satu bahasa, yang hanya berbeda namanya', p. 1); informants were all from (then) Kabupaten Kapuas — Kuala Kapuas, Mandomai (Pulau Petak), Pangkoh, Bukit Rawi, Kahayan Tengah and Pulang Pisau — with the main informant from Pulang Pisau on the lower Kahayan River (pp. 4-5); they recognise sub-dialects Kahayan-Kapuas Ngawa (downriver), Kahayan Ngaju and Kapuas Ngaju (upriver) (p. 21). So the statement is first-hand for lower Kahayan/Kapuas Ngaju speech c. 1990 and belongs with ngaj1237 (no separate Kahayan dialect node exists in current Glottolog, whose Ngaju dialects are Ba'amang, Mantangai, Pulopetak). Its second-syllable-from-the-left stress claim conflicts with the penultimate statements for Pulopetak Ngaju (Hardeland 1858; Mihing & Stokhof 1977) already in the catalog under ngaj1237 — flag, do not merge silently.

new_statements.quote: Jedes Wort hat nur auf einer Sylbe den Accent. Derselbe fällt, wie die vielen oben angegebenen Beispiele zeigen, auf die vorletzte Sylbe, die ja auch in der Regel die Hauptsylbe des Stammwortes ist. Wo indess, in durch Suffixe abgeleiteten Wörtern, diese Hauptsylbe zur drittletzten Sylbe wird, bleibt der Accent doch auf der Penultima, geht dann also von der ursprünglich betonten auf die tonlose Sylbe des Stammwortes über. — In reduplicirten oder zusammengesetzten Wörtern verliert das erste Glied den ursprünglichen Accent, da jedes Wort nur auf einer Sylbe den Accent hat. [p. 18] ... 1. der Accent bleibt auf der letzten Sylbe der wenigen einsylbigen Wörter, ... auch wenn dieselben durch Präfixe 2 oder mehrsylbig geworden sind; z. B. hai, gross, dick; kahai, Grösse; mampahai, vergrössern. [p. 18]
new_statements.translation: Every word has the accent on only one syllable. It falls, as the many examples given above show, on the penultimate syllable, which as a rule is also the main syllable of the root word. Where, however, in words derived by suffixes, this main syllable becomes the antepenult, the accent still stays on the penultima, and so passes from the originally accented syllable to the unaccented syllable of the root. — In reduplicated or compound words the first member loses its original accent, since every word has the accent on only one syllable. ... 1. the accent stays on the last syllable of the few monosyllabic words, ... even when they have become di- or polysyllabic through prefixes; e.g. hai, big, thick; kahai, size; mampahai, to enlarge.
new_statements.citation: Hardeland, August. 1858. Versuch einer Grammatik der Dajackschen Sprache. Amsterdam: Frederik Muller. ('Accent oder Betonung', pp. 18-19)

new_statements.relation_note: The existing statement (Durasid, Kawi & Djinal 1990: 46-47) gives phonetic main stress on the SECOND syllable from the beginning of the word, with /pa'hai/, /ta'pahai/, /mam'pahai/, /ta'karambang/, /ta'pakarambang/. Hardeland gives the PENULTIMATE syllable, kept on the penult under suffixation. The two coincide only for trisyllables (ta'pahai = penult); they differ for disyllables (Hardeland: initial/penult, e.g. tamä, asö; Durasid: second = final, e.g. /pa'hai/) and for 4+-syllable words (Hardeland: penult; Durasid: second from left, /ta'karambang/, /ta'pakarambang/ = pre-antepenult). Even on the shared item hai/pahai/mampahai they differ: Hardeland kahai, mampahai with FINAL accent (monos…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One accent per word, on the penultimate syllable; suffixation shifts the accent rightward so it stays on the penult (tamä > manämaän, käju > käjuan, tahi > katahian); in reduplications and compounds only the last member keeps its accent (bätängdänüm). The language described is 'Dajacksch' = Ngaju, on the Pulopetak dialect used for the Bible translation; Kahaian is named as one of four main dialects (pp. 8-9) with segmental peculiarities and 'hard, short, sharply clipped syllables, loud voice', but no separate accent rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the text says explicitly that a word has the accent on only one syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) The few monosyllabic words (hai, haus, etc.) keep final accent even when prefixed: kahai, mampahai; kahaus, mampahaus (the derivational penult then always has a short final vowel); also gantau 'right', kakai 'so', bewäi 'only' have final accent (the last two often spoken as monosyllables kai, wäi). (2) Antepenult accent only in hallai, sallai 'very', handiai, samandiai 'all', and in disyllables made trisyllabic by the suffixes -ku/-ngku (1st person) or -e (3rd person), which keep the accent on the originally accented syllable: asö 'dog' > asöngku 'my dog'; akü imükule 'I am beaten by him' (p. 19).
new_statements.identity_note: Hardeland 1858 describes the 'Dajacksche Sprache' of Middle-South Borneo = Ngaju Dayak, expressly on the Pulopetak dialect ('welchen Dialect ich beim Uebersetzen der Bibel gebraucht habe', p. 8). He distinguishes four main dialects, Pulopetak, Mangkatip, Mantangai and Kahaian (p. 8), and gives Kahaian only segmental peculiarities (r > l, g ~ k, dj ~ tj, b ~ w, ng before k) and the remark 'Der Kahaianer spricht hart, die Sylben kurz und scharf abgestossen, mit lauter Stimme' (p. 9); the accent section is not dialect-specific. Durasid et al. 1990 (Struktur Bahasa Kahayan) is the Kahayan-specific source and is 130 years later. kaha1240 is a Glottolog bookkeeping code (retired ISO [xah], merged into Ngaju [nij]).

readall_conflicts: Hardeland 1858 (pp. 18-19) states penultimate accent, retained on the penult under suffixation, with listed final-accent exceptions (prefixed monosyllables hai > kahai, mampahai; gantau, kakai, bewäi) and antepenult exceptions (hallai, sallai, handiai, samandiai; disyllable + -ku/-ngku/-e). Durasid, Kawi & Djinal 1990 (pp. 46-47), the only Kahayan-specific source, state phonetic main stress on the second syllable from the beginning (/pa'hai/, /mam'pahai/, /ta'karambang/, /ta'pakarambang/) and non-distinctive suprasegmentals. These agree only on trisyllables; they contradict on disyllables (penult = initial vs. second = final) and on 4-5-syllable words (penult vs. second from left = pre-antepenult), and on mampahai (Hardeland final, Durasid second). The disagreement is partly a dialect and register matter: Hardeland describes 19th-century Pulopetak Ngaju (the Bible dialect) and names Kahaian only as a dialect with segmental differences and no separate accent rule, while Durasid et al. explicitly call penultimate stress the church pastors' pattern that sounds awkward in Kahayan. The Kahayan-specific 1990 description is kept as the reading of record for kaha1240; Hardeland's penult rule belongs to Ngaju (ngaj1237) and is filed here as a contradicting older description of a different dialect.
